title: China’s First State IDs for AI Persons Enable Legal Business
summary:
A pilot program in Beijing is assigning official identity cards to AI-generated virtual influencers to allow them to conduct banking and enter contracts. These state-issued IDs include the persona's name, birthday, address, and facial features, providing the legal capacity to open digital-currency wallets and form commercial partnerships. Yuri, a popular virtual artist and idol, is among the first personas recognized as a "digital resident" in the capital.

The initiative targets a digital-human sector valued at over $10 billion with more than 1.3 million active firms. Supporters say the IDs protect intellectual property and hold creator companies accountable for virtual actions, though critics warn the system may expand government surveillance. Some companies now pay citizens up to $20,000 to license their physical likenesses for virtual replicas as China builds the legal infrastructure for an AI to AI economy.

China is officially issuing government ID cards to AI-generated “digital humans,” so virtual influencers can open bank accounts and conduct business. These state-issued IDs, which include a name, birthday, address, and facial features, give virtual personas the legal ability to open digital-currency wallets, sign contracts, and form commercial partnerships.

Among the first to receive this recognition is Yuri, a popular AI-generated virtual idol and artist, who is now officially recognized as a “digital resident” in Beijing. The step comes as China’s digital-human market expands, with more than 1.3 million active firms and a sector value past $10 billion.

Supporters describe the IDs as a way to protect intellectual property and hold creator companies legally accountable for virtual actions. Critics warn that placing synthetic entities in official state systems could expand government surveillance in the digital space. Some companies are offering everyday citizens up to $20,000 to license their physical likenesses for virtual replicas, which narrows the line around personal identity.

China’s move sets a precedent that other countries will have to meet when they decide how far AI should be given a legal status that resembles a human one.
